title: Elizabeth Fry
hookLine: a Quaker woman walks into the women's side of Newgate prison, sits down, and reads

cards: The door to the women's side of Newgate prison in London opens, and a woman in plain Quaker clothes steps through.
Inside, women awaiting trial and women already sentenced are crowded together, some with their children, short of clothes and short of hope.
The story told about that first visit is that the keepers warned her it wasn't safe, and that she went in anyway. She doesn't preach at anyone. She sits down.
She asks about the children. Her name is Elizabeth Fry, a wife, a mother, and a Quaker minister.

teach.h: THAT OF GOD IN EVERY ONE.
teach.b: Fry was a Quaker, a member of the Religious Society of Friends. Their founder, George Fox, told his followers to "walk cheerfully over the world, answering that of God in every one."
Every one: the woman in the next cell, and the woman who stole bread. Fry took it literally. She didn't start with a speech about reform.
She started a small school inside the prison for the children living there with their mothers. She brought in sewing and knitting so the women could work and earn something.
She gathered a group of women visitors who came back week after week.
And by the usual account, she asked the prisoners themselves to agree to the rules of the new arrangement, instead of handing rules down. Then she read, plainly, out loud, from the Bible.

teach.h: I WAS IN PRISON, AND YE CAME.
teach.b: Behind all of it sat a scene in Matthew where the king says to the righteous, in the King James Bible, "I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me."

The righteous ask when they ever did that, and he answers: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." To Fry, a prison visit was not charity from above.
It was meeting Christ in a cell. Her work spread beyond Newgate. She visited women on ships carrying convicts overseas, and spoke to members of Parliament about how prisons were run.
Churches still send visitors into prisons today, and the work still begins the same way: someone walks in and sits down.

how: In some churches, prison ministry teams visit people in jail, lead Bible studies, write letters and support families, often pointing to Matthew 25 as the reason.

practice: Write a few honest lines, on paper or in your head, to someone in prison: someone you know, or a stranger you'll never meet. No advice, no lecture, just: you're a person, and someone remembered you today.
Some churches and charities run letter programs, if you ever want to send it. If you pray, hold that person before God.

wordCard.voice: Elizabeth Fry. A Quaker minister who walked into Newgate, sat with the women and their children, and helped change how prisons treated them.
